newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mixed in US, Tietmeyer remarks boost mark.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in US, Tietmeyer remarks boost mark.

text.p: The dollar ended lower versus the mark after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the bank was not seeking further mark weakness, experts said.

But the dollar closed higher against the yen despite reports showing deterioration in the U.S. trade position relative to Japan. Remarks by a Commerce Department official helped soothe concern that the dollar was to blame for the trade figures.
The Tietmeyer comments were "a moderate statement of support for the mark," said Kevin Harris, an international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch.
Harris said: "If they don't want it (the mark) weaker, the two things that can happen are that it stays where it is or it gets stronger. And currencies rarely stay where they are."
The dollar closed at 1.7240/50 marks, down from 1.7269/74 at the open. Against the yen, the dollar finished at 125.90/95, up from 125.62/72.

During a news conference after the Bundesbank council's regularly scheduled meeting on Thursday, Tietmeyer said the mark's current level on foreign exchange markets correctly reflects economic fundamentals. He said the bank does not want a weak mark and remains interested in having a strong mark.

Initially, the dollar came under selling pressure overnight in Asia after the Japanese Ministry of Finance reported Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. ballooned 11.2 percent in March from a year earlier. By comparison, the overall Japanese customs-cleared trade surplus shrank 26.8 percent in March from a year ago.

Japanese trade data were followed on Thursday morning by a report showing the U.S. trade shortfall with Japan widened slightly in February from January. The overall U.S. trade gap narrowed 8.5 percent to $11.59 billion in February, wider than the $10.1 billion deficit expected by Wall Street economists.
Still Commerce undersecretary Everett Ehrlich told Reuters Financial Television on Thursday that the level of the dollar was not a major factor driving the trade figures.

The dollar, which had managed to inch up after the U.S. trade report, rose slightly higher after the undersecretary's remarks. The dollar also gained as investors continued to buy the currency to take advantage of the fact that interest rates in the U.S. remain well above those in Japan.
"To an extent, maybe there was a little bit of movement on Ehrlich," said David Solin, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
Solin also noted an ongoing interest to buy dollars and sell yen. "Again obviously, that's due to the big, wide rate differentials," he added.

The Bank of Japan has kept its official interest rates at record low levels to stimulate economic growth, but the Federal Reserve hiked the federal funds rate to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent on March 25 to keep inflationary pressures in check.
A currency trader at the New York branch of a Japanese bank said there was "pretty aggressive" buying of dollars below 125.50 yen by Japanese institutional investors.
In other trade, the dollar closed at 1.4635/45 Swiss francs, down from 1.4690/00 francs at the open.
The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3998/03 from C$1.3985/90.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7759/64, up from $0.7733/38.
